title: Raw tick values are not comparable across pools, so the annotated percentage is the only checkable part
content:
Three Uniswap v4 pools document an identical 0.1% band with entirely different numbers. PYUSD/USDS: "Min lower tick limit: 276,314 (-0.1%), Max upper tick limit: 276,334 (+0.1%)" (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.11.1.2.4.5). USDG/USDS: "-276,334 (-0.1%)" to "-276,314 (+0.1%)" (.11.3.2.4.5) — the same magnitudes with the sign flipped. rlUSD/USDS: "-10 (-0.1%)" to "10 (+0.1%)" (.11.4.2.4.5).

A Uniswap tick encodes the price of token1 in token0, so the value depends on which asset sorts first and on the two tokens' decimals. A ±276,324-centred band and a ±0 band can describe the same economic parity; the ~276,324 offset is the decimals gap between a 6-decimal and an 18-decimal token, and the sign follows the ordering.

The practical consequence is that the parenthesised percentages are doing the real work. Nothing else in the document lets a reader verify a tick value, and a sign or ordering mistake would place authorised liquidity on entirely the wrong side of parity while still looking like a plausible number.

The inconsistency extends to the field itself: PYUSD/USDS and USDT/USDS both specify "Max tick width: 10 ticks", while USDG/USDS and rlUSD/USDS omit the line. Whether the width constraint applies to those two pools cannot be determined from the Artifact — four instances of the same protocol, and half of them lack a parameter the other half treat as part of the risk configuration.
description: The same ±0.1% band appears as 276,314–276,334 in one pool, -276,334 to -276,314 in another and -10 to +10 in a third, because ticks depend on token ordering and decimals.
